title: Eternal rest
hookLine: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord

lines: A CARD AT THE BACK OF THE FUNERAL HOME.
A NAME, TWO DATES, FOUR LINES.
cards: A small card, the size of a playing card, left on a table at the back of a funeral home. On the front, a painting of Jesus or Mary. On the back, a name, two dates, and four short lines.
People slip these cards into wallets, Bibles and kitchen drawers, and find them years later, a little bent at the corners. The four lines are often the same, whoever's name is above them.
Catholics say them for the well-known and the forgotten alike.

teach.h: REQUIEM IS THE LATIN FOR REST.
teach.b: Here they are, in traditional English.

teach.h: REST AND LIGHT, ASKED FOR SOMEONE ELSE.
teach.b: "Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen." In Latin the prayer opens "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Requiem is the Latin for rest.

Those words also open the entrance chant of the Church's Mass for the dead, which is why that Mass, and music written for it, carry the name requiem. The prayer asks two gifts. Rest, after a life of work and worry.
And light after the dark of death: perpetual light, light that doesn't go out. It asks nothing for the person saying it; it's entirely for someone else. Why pray for the dead at all?
You met the answer in year two, in the second book of Maccabees, where Judas Maccabeus has prayers and sacrifice offered for fallen soldiers.
The Douay-Rheims closes the passage: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins."
The Catechism teaches that those who die in God's friendship but still need purifying can be helped by the prayers of the living.
Not every church counts Maccabees as scripture, or prays for the dead in this way, and that difference can be named plainly.

teach.h: A WEEK OF HOLDING PEOPLE UP.
teach.b: Last, look back at this week: pilgrims at Lourdes and Fatima, a local shrine, the incorruptibles, a votive candle, grace before meals, a cross on a child's forehead.

teach.h: LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.
teach.b: Again and again, someone was held up to God. Today's prayer is the same gesture, for people who can no longer ask for anything themselves.

how: Catholics say the Eternal Rest prayer for the dead at funerals, at graves, during November, after grace or the rosary, and whenever a person who has died is remembered. It is often printed on the back of funeral prayer cards.

games.q: you're holding a funeral prayer card for someone you barely knew. you turn it over and see the four lines. what do they ask for?
o: rest and perpetual light for the one who died.
that the dead be remembered by history.
games.why: "eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them." the whole prayer is for the dead.

practice: Let one name come to mind, someone who has died: a grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, someone you barely knew but haven't forgotten.
If you pray, say the four lines for them, then let another name come, and another; if you don't, say each name and leave a breath of quiet after it, like a candle left burning.
If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Requiem. Latin for rest, the first word of the Church's prayer for the dead and of the entrance chant at a Mass for the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, eternal rest: the opening words of the prayer for the dead.

carryVoice: Your line: let perpetual light shine. Rest, and a light that doesn't go out. See you tomorrow.
